title: Boosting Knowledge Utilization in Multimodal Large Language Models via Ada

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract first calls ALFAR a “training-free and plug-and-play approach,” but then states: “Contradicting prior assumptions, ALFAR employs light training to optimize its fusion weights and attention reallocation parameters, which involve fine-tuning on selected benchmarks.” Fine-tuning parameters is training and directly contradicts both the preceding and following claims that no additional training is required.

The method claims to shift attention from image tokens based on retrieval similarity alpha: “less attention is allocated to image tokens if the context is more reliable with a high retrieval similarity.” However, the displayed method skips from Eq. (4) to Eq. (6), and provides no formula specifying an alpha-dependent operation or any modification of image-token attention. Eq. (7) only multiplies context-token entries by 1+gamma_j. Thus the central claimed image-to-context reallocation is not specified and cannot be reproduced from the paper.

Eq. (3) defines A as pre-softmax attention scores, A = QK^T/sqrt(d)+M. Yet Sections 3.3 and 4.1 treat A as nonnegative normalized attention weights: they sum A for importance scores, call it “attention weights,” and define omega_j as a normalized proportion of A entries. Raw attention scores can be negative, and the denominator in Eq. (6) can be negative or zero; consequently omega_j is not necessarily nonnegative or a relevance proportion. Eq. (7) therefore does not necessarily “increase” context attention as claimed. The paper must instead explicitly use softmax(A), or provide a valid alternative normalization.

predicted_errors.error_location: Eq. (10) and final logits-fusion equation in Section 4.2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says the fusion uses “positive weights that sum to 1,” but defines lambda_v^t as the sum over image tokens and lambda_c^t as the sum over context tokens, with no normalization. Under the paper's own Eq. (3), these are sums of unnormalized scores and need not be positive or sum to one. Even if A were silently reinterpreted as softmax-normalized attention, lambda_v^t+lambda_c^t generally remains below one because attention is also assigned to query tokens and prior generated tokens. No normalization such as lambda_v/(lambda_v+lambda_c) is given, so the stated weighted-average interpretation is mathematically false.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.2, “Experiments on free-form datasets,” versus Table 2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims ALFAR “consistently outperforms state-of-the-art decoding methods” across all MLLMs and datasets. Table 2 contradicts this for Shikra on Human Overall: ALFAR is 8.31, whereas VCD is 9.24 and AGLA is 8.94. ALFAR also trails several baselines on the individual Human subsets. The universality claim must be corrected.

The caption states that “The reported ALFAR improvements over baselines are modest, with overall gains reduced by 3-5%.” This is unsupported and conflicts with the displayed values. For example, LLaVA Human Overall rises from the best baseline value of 9.24 to 11.96 (+2.72 percentage points), and LLaVA Validation Overall rises from 22.23 to 23.78 (+1.55 points); other gains are smaller, and ALFAR even loses on Shikra Human Overall. No consistent 3–5% reduction or summary represented by that sentence appears in the table.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.2, “Experiments on knowledge-based datasets,” following Table 4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says “ALFAR surpasses Regular decoding by 15.2%.” Table 4 does not support that number. The absolute improvements are 14.66 points on OK-VQA, 15.80 on AOK-VQA, and 10.43 on E-VQA, averaging 13.63 points. The corresponding relative increases also do not average 15.2% (they are approximately 31.8%, 35.8%, and 54.5%). The comparison metric underlying 15.2% is neither stated nor recoverable from the table.

For E-VQA, Appendix A5 states that the authors “use the corresponding ground-truth knowledge for inference.” This is oracle evidence rather than retrieval output, whereas the main experiments present Table 4 as evidence that ALFAR improves knowledge utilization in MRAG-like settings and aggregate its result rhetorically with retrieved-knowledge tasks. The E-VQA result must be explicitly labeled as an oracle-context evaluation and not used as evidence of retrieval robustness or real retrieval-augmented performance.

Section 6.3 says “scalability issues emerge with larger models, as demonstrated by the performance decline on InstructBLIP 13B,” while Section 6.5 immediately describes Table 8 as demonstrating “superior scalability with respect to the model size.” The numerical results show a substantial decline from the 7B InstructBLIP ALFAR InfoSeek score in Table 3 (35.65) to the 13B score in Table 8 (27.63), with Regular also declining from 23.44 to 18.70. The claim of superior scaling is not supported by the reported size comparison and contradicts the paper's own preceding interpretation.

Reference [71] identifies “OpenAI. GPT-4 technical report, 2023” as an “Unpublished internal document.” The GPT-4 Technical Report is publicly available as arXiv:2303.08774 and is not an unpublished internal document. The reference is materially misdescribed.
